set.story: The Greek philosopher Plato, writing around 360 BCE, described Atlantis, a rich and powerful island nation that sank into the sea in a single day and night. Most scholars believe he invented it as a moral tale about pride and power.

why: 'Scholars agree' overstates consensus, and the lesson is about hubris/the ideal state rather than 'government' generally

set.story: “Kumbaya” (“come by here”) is an African American spiritual, first recorded in 1926, asking God to come and help people in need. It became a popular campfire song and was sung in the civil rights movement in the 1950s and 1960s; later, people began using it to mock calls for easy harmony.

why: Campfire popularity began in the late 1950s (Folksmiths 1957, Song Sampler 1956), not only the 1960s

set.story: In the 1750s, Benjamin Franklin promoted the lightning rod, a metal rod on a roof that catches lightning strikes and carries the electricity safely into the ground.

why: A lightning rod intercepts strikes that would hit the building; it does not meaningfully 'attract' lightning

set.story: In folklore around the world, the bogeyman is a monster with no fixed appearance that adults say will come for children who misbehave. Spanish-speaking countries have a similar figure called El Coco or El Cuco.

why: Bogeyman has no specific appearance rather than being 'shapeless'; 'bugbear' is too rare for a level-2 learner and today mostly means a pet peeve

ex: A surgeon, jazz pianist and published poet, Dr. Okafor is a true Renaissance man.
Wei is a Renaissance man who builds furniture, speaks four languages and writes code.

why: 'all-rounder' is chiefly British (spec requires American usage); second example used 'Renaissance woman' instead of the term

ex: After his release from prison, Liam stayed on the straight and narrow, working two jobs and saving money.
The coach kept her young players on the straight and narrow with strict curfews and study hours.

cloze.s: Her mentor helped her quit gambling and stay on ___ for good.

why: Avoid pairing a Latino name with prison and an East Asian name with gambling (stereotype risk)

ex: The star chef’s fall from grace began when health inspectors shut down his flagship restaurant.
Once the league’s top scorer, the striker suffered a fall from grace after failing a drug test.

why: Avoid pairing a name associated with a specific group with a failed drug test (stereotype risk)

ex: Randomized studies that compare a drug with a fake pill are the gold standard for testing new medicines.
Her hotel’s customer service has become the gold standard in the industry.

why: The gold-standard trial is defined by randomization and control, not size; 'large studies' was inaccurate
Recruiters can plausibly call an elusive dream candidate their 'white whale', so it can fill the cloze
'unicorn' (rare, hard-to-find thing) can sensibly fill 'has been Jamal’s ___' and overlaps the elusive-goal sense
Pundits are known for making predictions; tempting overlap with 'a person who claims to predict the future'

ex: When the product failed, the CEO told reporters, “The buck stops here,” and apologized.
As team captain, Aisha tells her teammates after every loss that the buck stops here, with her.

why: Second example used 'the buck stops with her', which does not contain the full term
